name: Qizhi Weitong granules (Chinese herbal formula)
short: Contains Corydalis (high liver-injury risk signal in national reaction data; 2 liver cases with a corydalis sleep aid), licorice, Bupleurum. 197 with dyspepsia: no more adverse effects than placebo.
text: Studies: in a randomized, double-blind, multicentre trial in 197 people with the postprandial distress type of functional dyspepsia, which set out to study safety as well as efficacy, the granules did not cause more adverse effects than placebo over 4 weeks; the abstract does not give event numbers or types. A 2022 meta-analysis of the granules added to mosapride, compared with mosapride alone, found no significant difference in safety. A 2022 health technology assessment of four Chinese patent medicines for functional dyspepsia (30 of 110 studies on these granules, tablets or capsules), of generally low-quality literature, reports no serious adverse reactions for the four medicines, without giving results for each. A 2025 network meta-analysis of 12 Chinese patent medicines added to conventional medicine in functional dyspepsia found no regimen with a significant increase in adverse events, except a higher risk with another patent capsule than with these granules, each added to conventional medicine (odds ratio 4.82, 95% CI 1.02 to 22.87, a wide interval). Herbs: a laboratory study in mice describes the formula (as "particles") as composed of six plants: Bupleurum chinense, a peony (Paeonia obovata), bitter orange (Citrus aurantium), licorice (Glycyrrhiza uralensis), Cyperus rotundus and Corydalis rhizome (the abstract names the plant part only for Corydalis); a laboratory study in rats names a Corydalis alkaloid as a major component of the formula, and a quality-control study of the granules measured glycyrrhizic acid and a licorice glycoside in them. Corydalis and the liver (neither abstract names these granules): a signal-detection study of national adverse drug reaction monitoring data (the abstract does not name the country), which combined reporting odds ratios with network toxicology and computational chemistry and checked the results against typical clinical cases, identified Corydalis rhizome as a traditional Chinese medicine with a high risk of liver injury; separately, a report of 2 cases describes liver injury in people taking a sleep aid containing corydalis, marketed by cannabis dispensaries (a different product): in an asymptomatic woman, liver enzymes rose and fell on taking and retaking it, and in a man with symptoms consistent with liver dysfunction, liver function returned to normal after stopping. Licorice and Bupleurum (Japanese reporting data; neither abstract names these granules): in analyses of the Japanese adverse drug event report database, the risk of pseudoaldosteronism rose with licorice intake from herbal medicines, and reporting signals for drug-induced interstitial lung disease, which the authors call a severe adverse event, were found for 32 of 54 herbal medicines, including Bupleurum root (the mouse study does not name the part of Bupleurum in the formula); the abstract gives adjusted reporting odds ratios for Scutellaria root and Pinellia tuber but none for Bupleurum root, and the authors conclude that the lung disease was dose-dependent on the crude drugs; reports of this kind cannot show cause. PubMed searches found no report of liver injury, kidney injury or heavy-metal contamination naming these granules themselves. No interaction data were found in the cited sources; the granules were given with mosapride in the pooled trials, and that meta-analysis abstract reports no interaction.
